section_summary: This section moves from 1941 assessments of Japanese and Japanese-American newspapers—including censorship of the Japan News Week and the political alignment of the Japan Times and Advertiser—to wartime correspondence about press consolidation, historical newspaper issues, and overseas Japanese news services. Most of the section consists of November 1943 Dōmei Agency bulletins circulated in Turkey, combining exaggerated Japanese victory claims with reports promoting the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, collaborationist governments, Indian independence, and Japanese administration in occupied territories. The bulletins also document Japanese propaganda concerning the Greater East Asia Conference, fighting around Bougainville and New Guinea, and political developments across East and Southeast Asia.

subfiles.title: Review of Japanese and Japanese-American press coverage
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese press arguments on China, Australia, Japanese-American relations, and the American national emergency, followed by an assessment of Japanese-American publications.
subfiles.summary: The review records claims that Japan would permit Western enterprise in China, that Australia favored cooperation, and that a U.S.–Japan agreement could end the China conflict. It then summarizes the Japanese American’s coverage of Roosevelt’s emergency declaration and alleged American opposition to war. The concluding comment distinguishes the overtly American-oriented propaganda of the Japanese American Review from the Japanese American’s appeal to older immigrants through pan-Asian and Buddhist themes.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1446 concerning censorship of the Japan News Week
subfiles.about: Reports official threats against editor Ward H. Wills after an editorial criticized Hitler and suggested that Nazi Germany might be defeated.
subfiles.summary: Japanese censors initially passed foreign dispatches describing the Japan News Week editorial, but the published issue was subsequently banned. Officials told Wills that the article attacked Japan’s fundamental policy and warned that continued criticism could lead to suppression or imprisonment. Wills defended independent editorial judgment and said he would cease publication rather than turn the newspaper into a propaganda sheet.

subfiles.title: Memorandum and Millard letter excerpt on the Japan Times and Advertiser
subfiles.about: Assesses Thomas Millard’s claim that Matsuoka-aligned interests purchased the Japan Advertiser to influence Japanese foreign policy.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum finds the claim plausible, noting Toshi Go’s ties to Matsuoka and the South Manchuria Railway. Millard’s excerpt describes attempts by the Times and Advertiser to promote Matsuoka, a U.S. visit, cooperation over China, and compromise with Chiang Kai-shek. It concludes that the Japanese military retained control of Tokyo’s government and foreign policy.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference for Kaigai Dōbō
subfiles.about: Points to a translated copy of the first issue of Kaigai Dōbō, published by the Overseas Japanese Central Society.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references a Justice Department letter dated October 11, 1941. It identifies the referenced item as a translation of Kaigai Dōbō’s first issue, dated July 15, 1941, and directs readers to the Overseas Japanese Central Society file.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference for Japanese seven-point program
subfiles.about: Cross-references instructions for commenting on a truculent seven-point Japanese program published in the Japan Times and Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: The sheet describes a Japanese seven-point list of demands intended to resolve tensions with the United States. It points to telegram 4716 of November 5, 1941, which suggested emphasizing to the Foreign Office the uncompromising tone of Japanese press articles.

subfiles.title: Amalgamation of the Tokyo Nichi Nichi and Osaka Mainichi
subfiles.from: James W. Gantenbein, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Reports that two major Japanese newspapers merged as the Mainichi Shimbun, probably because of paper shortages.
subfiles.summary: A local Japanese-language report stated that the Tokyo Nichi Nichi Shimbun and Osaka Mainichi Shimbun began appearing under the Mainichi Shimbun name on January 1, 1943. The embassy suggests that wartime paper shortages probably caused the consolidation and identifies Saburo Suzuki as the Buenos Aires representative of both former papers.

subfiles.title: Lillian J. Mitchell’s letter sending 1920 Japan Advertiser issues
subfiles.about: Offers several 1920 newspaper issues whose editorial discussion of land ownership in Japan might interest the President.
subfiles.summary: Mitchell states that she is mailing separately several old newspapers from 1920. She especially calls attention to an editorial dealing with land in Japan and offers encouragement to Roosevelt during a time of trial.

subfiles.title: Analysis of October 1920 Japan Advertiser issues
subfiles.about: Reviews the editorials and translated articles in the newspaper issues supplied by Lillian J. Mitchell.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum highlights a Tokyo Nichinichi editorial urging moderation over American land and immigration laws and asking how Japan would respond to foreign landholding or mass Chinese immigration into Hokkaido. Other issues cover the Hunchun Incident, criticize Japanese incursions into China, and reproduce a missionary’s account of harsh treatment of Koreans. The newspapers are judged historically significant because they contrast Japan’s relatively critical press mood in 1920 with that of the preceding decade.

subfiles.title: Reply to Lillian J. Mitchell
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Mitchell’s letter and the October 1920 Japan Advertiser issues she supplied.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that Mitchell’s letter to the President and the newspapers sent separately were referred to it. Salisbury thanks her for the helpful spirit in which she brought the material to the government’s attention.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese foreign-language newspapers in occupied territories
subfiles.about: Relays a German press report on Japanese agencies’ extensive foreign-language newspaper operations in occupied Asia.
subfiles.summary: The report enumerates Dōmei, Asahi, and Mainichi newspapers in Singapore, Malaya, Java, the Philippines, Celebes, and Hainan. It identifies the Manila, Java, Celebes, and Shōnan Shimbun as especially important and explains that foreign-language evening papers reused news from Japanese-language morning editions. English-language papers were reportedly considered temporary.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning Dōmei News Bulletins from Turkey
subfiles.about: Advises that Washington already receives equivalent Dōmei material through federal broadcast-monitoring reports.
subfiles.summary: Kohler explains that the Division of Japanese Affairs checked whether Berry’s Dōmei bulletins provided unique information. The Federal Communications Commission’s Broadcast Intelligence Service already issued daily reports covering the same material for Washington agencies, including the State Department.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Japanese Dōmei News Bulletins in Turkey
subfiles.from: Burton Y. Berry, American Consul General, Istanbul
subfiles.about: Forwards privately obtained November issues of the Japanese Dōmei news bulletin and asks whether the Department already receives the information elsewhere.
subfiles.summary: Berry transmits copies of daily Japanese Dōmei bulletins issued in Turkey during November. He notes that they include subjects beyond military communiqués and hopes the private source will continue to provide them. He requests guidance if the Department already receives equivalent reporting.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Information Bulletin, Ankara, November 4—French edition
subfiles.about: Reports Fascist organization in Japan, Free India diplomacy, military claims in Burma, fundraising in Malaya, physical education in Indochina, and Japanese–Thai cooperation.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin says Italian Fascists in Kobe reorganized under Gennaro Liguori and that the Free India government thanked Mitsuru Tōyama and Chu Minyi. It claims a Japanese victory near Myitkyina and describes Overseas Chinese fundraising for Japanese aircraft in Johor Bahru. Further items praise physical education in French Indochina and commemorate the Japan–Thailand Society.

subfiles.title: Dōmei News Bulletin, Ankara, November 4—English edition
subfiles.about: Combines diplomatic, military, ideological, and economic reports from China, Burma, the South Pacific, and Celebes.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin reports Masayuki Tani’s arrival in Shanghai and repeats Japanese claims concerning Tankakok, Trangen Island, and Pomele. A Shanghai editorial depicts the Sino-Japanese alliance as the route to Chinese independence from Anglo-American influence. A lengthy Makassar item portrays Japanese administration as bringing agricultural, industrial, educational, and cultural progress to Manado and Minahasa.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Information Bulletin on the Greater East Asia Conference
subfiles.about: Describes the Greater East Asia Conference in Tokyo and reproduces the central themes of speeches by Tōjō and Wang Jingwei.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin details the seating, delegates, translation arrangements, and ceremonial atmosphere of the conference attended by Japan and allied Asian regimes. Tōjō denounces Anglo-American colonialism and presents Japan as the architect of a new East Asian order. Wang Jingwei praises Japan, invokes Sun Yat-sen, and advocates political sovereignty, cultural development, diplomatic harmony, and mutual economic assistance.

subfiles.title: Dōmei News Bulletin, Ankara, November 5—South Pacific military commentary
subfiles.about: Presents Japanese claims about ground and naval operations in the Solomon Islands and argues that Allied supply lines made their South Pacific campaign untenable.
subfiles.summary: A field report claims that a Japanese reconnaissance party repelled a larger force near Choiseul without casualties. Two commentaries describe Finschhafen, Bougainville, Rabaul, and Buin as scenes of disastrous Allied attacks. The analysis emphasizes allegedly overstretched American supply lines and asserts continuing Japanese command of the sea.

subfiles.title: Dōmei News Bulletin, Ankara, November 8, with erratum
subfiles.about: Claims sweeping Japanese naval victories, announces the proposed transfer of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to Free India, and reports political activity across East and Southeast Asia.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin gives inflated totals for Allied ships and aircraft allegedly destroyed around Bougainville and Rabaul. It reports Tōjō’s promise to transfer the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to Subhas Chandra Bose’s government, Lin Posheng’s arrival in Tokyo, Indian nationalist mobilization in Padang, and Emilio Abello’s support for the Greater East Asia Conference. A final erratum changes “battle cruiser” to “heavy cruiser.”

subfiles.title: Detached Dōmei bulletin leaf on Ichang and Haiphong
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese counterattacks near Ichang and an American air raid on Haiphong.
subfiles.summary: The fragment claims Japanese units repelled two attacks near Lungchuanpao and recovered weapons and ammunition from the battlefield. It also states that six American P-40 aircraft strafed the outskirts of Haiphong without causing Japanese losses.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Information Bulletin on the Battle of Bougainville
subfiles.about: Publishes an Imperial General Headquarters communiqué claiming major naval and air victories around Bougainville.
subfiles.summary: The communiqué describes attacks on Allied convoys and warships between Mono and Bougainville from October 31 through November 3. It claims numerous cruisers and destroyers sunk or damaged and reports fighting around Torokina. It also alleges that Japanese air and antiaircraft forces destroyed 200 aircraft at Rabaul and another 39 at Buka.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Information Bulletin, Ankara, November 8—French edition
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese air operations, Indian nationalist activity, an Italian Fascist office in Tokyo, and preparations for a Greater East Asia press conference.
subfiles.summary: Military items claim successful Japanese attacks at Nadzab, Finschhafen, Munda, Biloa, Vella Lavella, and Torokina. The bulletin praises financial and volunteer support for Free India among Indians in Saigon. It also reports Omero Principini’s new office for Italian Fascist interests and the passage through Shōnan of southern journalists bound for Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Dōmei News Bulletin, Ankara, November 8—English edition
subfiles.about: Covers Shanghai finance, Manchukuo diplomacy, Japanese air claims in New Guinea, and the training of Malay auxiliaries in Shōnan.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin reports the reopening of Shanghai’s clearing house and Zhang Jinghui’s return to Hsinking. It gives detailed but propagandistic figures for Japanese raids on Nadzab and fighting near Finschhafen. A long feature portrays Malay heiho auxiliaries as enthusiastic, disciplined, physically fit, and well cared for by Japanese commanders.

subfiles.title: Dōmei News Bulletin, Ankara, November 9
subfiles.about: Reports Philippine economic rhetoric, Japanese claims of American naval defeat, and the creation of provincial councils under occupation in Sumatra.
subfiles.summary: Benigno Aquino urges Filipinos to pair political independence with economic stability and sacrifice. Tokyo commentary treats American silence as proof of disastrous losses around the Solomons and gives enormous totals of ships and aircraft allegedly destroyed. The Sumatra item advertises provincial councils and welfare bureaus as evidence of Japanese-sponsored self-government, while retaining military control.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Information Bulletin, Ankara, November 10—Bougainville supplement
subfiles.about: Adds further Japanese victory claims for Bougainville and records congratulatory and propaganda reactions in Japan, Chungking, and Burma.
subfiles.summary: Imperial Headquarters claims another battleship sunk and additional cruisers damaged in the “Second Air Battle of Bougainville.” Tadahiko Okada congratulates Admiral Koga, while the bulletin interprets Reuters’ transmission of the claims as reluctant Chungking recognition of Japanese accuracy. An Indian National Army officer in Rangoon welcomes the promised transfer of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to Free India.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Information Bulletin on Free India recognition and regional news
subfiles.about: Reports Italian Fascist recognition of Free India, revised Japanese air claims, and a planned medical conference in Manila.
subfiles.summary: Omero Principini completes the process by which the Italian Fascist Republican Government recognizes the Provisional Government of Free India. Military notices raise the claimed number of Allied aircraft lost at Rabaul and report an interception over Ambon. José Laurel accepts the presidency of a Greater East Asian medical-scientific conference proposed for Manila.

subfiles.title: Dōmei News Bulletin, Ankara, November 10
subfiles.about: Reports official congratulations and presents Wang Jingwei’s and Zhang Jinghui’s ideological defenses of the Greater East Asia Conference.
subfiles.summary: Zhang Jinghui, Tadahiko Okada, and Tōjō send messages celebrating the conference declaration and Japanese naval claims. Wang Jingwei contrasts the conference’s stated principles with the Vienna and Versailles settlements and urges Chongqing to abandon the Anglo-Americans. Zhang similarly describes the Tokyo meeting as a sincere alliance against imperialism and predicts victory under Japanese leadership.

subfiles.title: Dōmei News Bulletin, Ankara, November 11
subfiles.about: Describes public celebration of Japanese victory claims, diplomatic congratulations, Bose’s anti-British speech, Macao currency controls, and estimates of Allied casualties.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin portrays Filipinos as jubilant over Japanese claims from Bougainville and records Zhang Jinghui’s congratulations to Japan’s military leaders. Subhas Chandra Bose rejects compromise with Britain at a Tokyo gathering, while a separate item notes Macao’s prohibition of Chinese twenty-cent coins. A lengthy calculation estimates more than 10,000 Allied personnel lost, using speculative crew figures for ships Japan claimed to have sunk.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Information Bulletin, Ankara, November 11
subfiles.about: Reports fighting near Bougainville and in Hunan, Bose’s visits to Japanese admirals, Manchukuo congratulations, and Philippine constitutional festivities.
subfiles.summary: Military notices announce another fleet action off Bougainville and describe a Japanese advance in the Dongting Lake region toward Hungmiao and Shihih. Bose visits Admirals Nagano and Shimada to congratulate them on Japanese naval claims. Additional items report Zhang Jinghui’s message to Tōjō and plans for a three-day celebration of the Philippine Republic’s constitution in Manila.

subfiles.title: Dōmei News Bulletin, Ankara, November 12
subfiles.about: Covers a Greater East Asian youth conference and ceremonies commemorating Sun Yat-sen in occupied China and Shōnan.
subfiles.summary: Youth representatives from Japan, Manchukuo, China, Burma, and the Hitler Youth meet at the Nippon Seinen Kaikan in Tokyo. In Nanking, Wang Jingwei uses Sun Yat-sen’s birthday to praise war against Britain and the United States, the Sino-Japanese alliance, and the recent conference declaration. Shanghai, Peking, and Shōnan hold parallel ceremonies interpreted as support for the collaborationist order.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Information Bulletin, Ankara, November 12—French edition
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese action in Central China and collaborationist commemorations of Sun Yat-sen in Nanking and Canton.
subfiles.summary: The military item claims the annihilation of roughly 500 Chinese troops southwest of Witachi. The political reports portray the Nanking government’s alliance with Japan and the Greater East Asia declaration as fulfilling Sun Yat-sen’s ideals. Ceremonies are described in Nanking and Canton, with Wang Jingwei and Japanese diplomatic representatives in attendance.

subfiles.title: Dōmei News Bulletin, Ankara, November 13
subfiles.about: Reports Indian military trainees, Philippine family statistics, and allegations of hostility between American and Chungking air officers.
subfiles.summary: Subhas Chandra Bose is said to have selected six Penang youths for military training in Japan, while a Manila item summarizes household-size statistics. The main article presents testimony from a captured Chinese lieutenant alleging American arrogance, refusal to engage Japanese raids, and violent quarrels with Chinese air officers at Yunnanyi. The account is plainly designed to undermine Sino-American military cooperation.

subfiles.title: Dōmei News Bulletin, Ankara, November 15
subfiles.about: Combines reports of Japanese operations in Hebei and the Solomons with Mamoru Shigemitsu’s ideological address on Asian independence.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin claims the capture of Wang Lienfang during a raid on an Eighth Route Army headquarters and successful Japanese air attacks on Mono and Torokina. In Osaka, Shigemitsu calls the Greater East Asia declaration a charter for a new world and depicts the war as Asia’s struggle for independence from Anglo-American colonialism. His speech argues that Japanese leadership, regional unity, and the justice of the cause guarantee victory.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Information Bulletin, Ankara, November 16—condolences and military reports
subfiles.about: Reports imperial condolences for the French ambassador and Japanese military claims from Hunan, Ichang, and Haiphong.
subfiles.summary: The emperor and empress send representatives or messages to the French Embassy after Ambassador Charles Arsène-Henry’s death. Military reports claim Japanese successes along the Canton–Hankou railway and near Yueyang, Taolin, Ichang, and Lungchuanpao. A final item says American P-40 aircraft strafed Haiphong without inflicting Japanese damage.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Information Bulletin, Ankara, November 16—evening reports
subfiles.about: Reports South Pacific air operations, an action against Communist troops in Hebei, honors for Javanese leaders, telegraph expansion, and Japanese naval appointments.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin claims successful attacks around the Gilbert, Bougainville, Mono, and Ellice islands and the capture of Wang Lienfang in Hebei. It announces Japanese decorations for Sukarno and other members of Java’s Central Council and an imperial audience for Sukarno. Other notices concern telegraph services in Bohol and Tarlac and new appointments at Sasebo and Imperial Naval Aviation Headquarters.

subfiles.title: Dōmei Information Bulletin, Ankara, November 17
subfiles.about: Announces another purported Japanese air victory off Bougainville and reports interceptions near Madang, Nauru, Hanoi, and Hong Kong.
subfiles.summary: Imperial Headquarters claims Japanese naval aircraft sank three aircraft carriers and other warships south of Bougainville in the so-called Fifth Air Battle off the island. Further notices claim Allied bombers shot down near Madang and Nauru. Reports from Hanoi and Hong Kong state that American aircraft were driven off by Japanese and allied defenses.

subfiles.title: Dōmei News Bulletin, Ankara, November 17—English edition
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese cabinet appointments, expands victory claims from Bougainville, and announces a new Thai military attaché in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The government appoints Teiichi Suzuki, Yoshisuke Aikawa, and Keita Gotō as cabinet advisers following Ginjirō Fujiwara’s resignation. Naval authorities describe an allegedly decisive attack on an Allied carrier force south of Bougainville and compile enormous ship and aircraft loss totals for the preceding twenty days. A Bangkok item announces Nomsak Pholarak’s appointment as Thai military attaché in Tokyo in place of Solakit Phisien.
